q.q: Which unit is defined as exactly 2²⁰ bytes in the 1024-based system used for CCEA answers?
o: Kilobyte
Megabyte
Gigabyte
Terabyte
q.why: 1 MB = 2²⁰ = 1 048 576 bytes. A kilobyte is 2¹⁰ bytes and a gigabyte is 2³⁰ bytes.

q.q: A video file is 6 MB. What is its size in KB, using 1024-based units?
q.why: Moving to a smaller unit means multiplying by 1024: 6 × 1024 = 6144 KB. 6 291 456 is the size in bytes.

q.q: A drive sold as 1 TB holds 10¹² bytes, but the operating system reports about 931 GB. What is the main reason?
o: Formatting the drive permanently uses up about 7% of it
The OS reserves part of the drive for the file allocation table
The OS counts in powers of 1024, the maker in powers of 1000
The drive stores data in nibbles rather than in whole bytes
q.why: Manufacturers use 1 TB = 10¹² bytes; an OS counting 1 GB as 2³⁰ bytes shows 10¹² ÷ 2³⁰ ≈ 931.

q.q: How many different values can be represented with 10 bits?
q.why: n bits give 2ⁿ patterns: 2¹⁰ = 1024. 1023 is the largest unsigned value, not the number of values.

q.q: What is the largest unsigned integer that can be stored in 12 bits?
q.why: The largest unsigned value is 2ⁿ − 1 = 2¹² − 1 = 4095, because one of the 4096 patterns is zero.

q.q: A program must store whole numbers from 0 to 512 inclusive. What is the minimum number of bits needed?
q.why: 0 to 512 is 513 values. 2⁹ = 512 is one too few, so 10 bits (1024 values) are needed.

q.q: Why is the largest unsigned value that n bits can hold 2ⁿ − 1 rather than 2ⁿ?
o: The most significant bit is reserved as a sign bit
One of the 2ⁿ patterns is used to represent zero
One pattern is kept back to signal an overflow
The last bit of every pattern is used for parity
q.why: There are 2ⁿ patterns, and 0 takes one of them, so the counting stops at 2ⁿ − 1.

q.q: What is the unsigned binary number 10011101 in denary?
q.why: 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 157. 185 comes from reading the bits in reverse.

q.q: What is 214 as an 8-bit unsigned binary number?
q.why: 214 = 128 + 64 + 16 + 4 + 2, giving 11010110. 01101011 is the same bits reversed.

q.q: 77 is converted by repeated division by 2. The remainders, in the order they are produced, are 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1. What is the 8-bit result?
q.why: Remainders are read from last to first: 1001101, padded to 01001101 (64 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 77). 01011001 is the top-down reading.

q.q: Which statement about an 8-bit unsigned binary number is correct?
o: An odd number always has a 1 in the least significant bit
An odd number always has a 1 in the most significant bit
The most significant bit has a place value of 256
The least significant bit has a place value of 2
q.why: The LSB is worth 1, so it is the only bit that can make a number odd. The MSB of a byte is worth 128.

q.q: What is the hexadecimal value 3C in 8-bit binary?
q.why: Each hex digit becomes one nibble: 3 = 0011 and C (12) = 1100.

q.q: What is 94 in hexadecimal?
o: 5D
E5
4E
5E
q.why: 94 ÷ 16 = 5 remainder 14, and 14 is E, so 94 = 5E.

q.q: A technician says, 'We store data in hexadecimal because it saves memory.' Which response is correct?
o: True, because each hex digit needs fewer bits than a denary digit
True, but only for colour codes and MAC addresses
Hex is only a notation for people; the value is still stored in binary
False, because hex needs more bits than the same value in binary
q.why: Hex makes binary shorter for humans to read and copy, but the computer always holds the bits themselves.

q.q: A MAC address is 48 bits long. How many hexadecimal digits are needed to write it?
q.why: One hex digit is one nibble (4 bits): 48 ÷ 4 = 12. Six is the number of bytes.

q.q: What is the year 1945 in binary-coded decimal?
q.why: Each denary digit is coded separately: 1 = 0001, 9 = 1001, 4 = 0100, 5 = 0101. 0111 1001 1001 is 1945 in pure binary.

q.q: The byte 01011001 represents 59 in BCD. What does the same byte represent as a pure unsigned binary number?
q.why: As pure binary, 64 + 16 + 8 + 1 = 89. BCD reads each nibble as a separate digit instead.

q.q: Why is BCD often used to hold amounts of money?
o: Each denary digit is held exactly, avoiding binary-fraction rounding
It uses less storage than the same value held in pure binary
Its arithmetic is simpler than arithmetic on pure binary
It can store negative amounts without needing a sign bit
q.why: Values such as 0.1 have no exact binary form, but BCD stores each denary digit as it is. BCD actually wastes storage and needs correcting arithmetic.

q.q: How many bits does 87 need in BCD compared with pure unsigned binary?
o: 7 bits in BCD and 8 bits in pure binary
8 bits in BCD and 8 bits in pure binary
4 bits in BCD and 7 bits in pure binary
8 bits in BCD and 7 bits in pure binary
q.why: BCD needs a nibble per digit: 1000 0111. In pure binary 87 = 1010111, which is 7 bits.

q.q: What is 01101101 + 00111011 as an 8-bit unsigned result?
q.why: 109 + 59 = 168 = 128 + 32 + 8 = 10101000. Checking in denary confirms the carries were handled correctly.

q.q: 190 and 90 are added in an 8-bit unsigned register. What value is left in the register?
q.why: 280 needs nine bits (100011000); only the lower eight bits, 00011000 = 24, are kept, so overflow has occurred.

q.q: In one column of a binary addition you add 1 + 0 with a carry in of 1. What do you write and carry?
o: Write 1, carry 0
Write 1, carry 1
Write 0, carry 0
Write 0, carry 1
q.why: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2 = 10 in binary, so write 0 and carry 1.

q.q: How many carries are generated when 00001111 is added to 00000001?
q.why: The carry ripples through each of the four 1s: 1111 + 1 = 10000, with a carry out of each of the lowest four columns.

q.q: What is −37 in 8-bit sign and magnitude?
q.why: Sign bit 1 for negative, then 37 = 0100101 in seven bits. 11011011 is −37 in two's complement.

q.q: Which byte represents 'negative zero' in 8-bit sign and magnitude?
q.why: A sign bit of 1 with a magnitude of 0000000 gives −0, a second pattern for zero.

q.q: In 8-bit sign and magnitude, 00000101 is added to 10000011 with an ordinary binary adder. What value does the result represent?
q.why: The sum is 10001000, which in sign and magnitude is −8, not the correct +2. This is why addition fails when signs differ.

q.q: Where is the sign-and-magnitude idea still used today?
o: Integer addition in a modern processor's ALU
Storing negative numbers on the address bus
The sign bit of an IEEE 754 floating-point number
Character codes in extended ASCII code pages
q.why: IEEE 754 stores the sign separately, as sign and magnitude does; integer arithmetic uses two's complement.

q.q: What is the byte 10000000 in 8-bit two's complement?
q.why: The MSB is worth −128 and no other bits are set. Two's complement has no negative zero.

q.q: What is the range of a 12-bit two's complement integer?
q.why: n bits give −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1: −2¹¹ = −2048 to 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047.

q.q: The byte 11001010 is read as an 8-bit two's complement integer. What is its value?
q.why: −128 + 64 + 8 + 2 = −54. −74 is the sign-and-magnitude reading and 202 the unsigned reading.

q.q: What is the main reason processors use two's complement for integers?
o: It can store larger positive numbers than unsigned binary
It has two patterns for zero, so zero tests are simpler
One adder circuit can carry out both addition and subtraction
The sign is held separately, so values are easy to read
q.why: A − B is done as A + (−B), so no separate subtracter or sign-comparison logic is needed. It has only one zero.

q.q: What is −37 in 8-bit two's complement?
q.why: 37 = 00100101; invert to 11011010; add 1 to get 11011011. 11011010 is the result of forgetting to add 1.

q.q: What is −100 in 8-bit two's complement?
What is the two's complement byte 10110110 in denary?
q.why: −128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = −74. −54 is the sign-and-magnitude reading and 182 the unsigned one.

q.q: Using the shortcut (copy bits from the right up to and including the first 1, then invert the rest), what is the two's complement of 00101000?
q.why: Keep '1000' and invert '0010' to '1101', giving 11011000 = −40. 11010111 is only the inversion.

q.q: To calculate 60 − 23 in 8-bit two's complement, which two bytes are added?
q.why: 60 = 00111100 and −23 = 11101001 (23 = 00010111, inverted and plus 1). 11101000 forgets the +1; 10010111 is sign and magnitude.

q.q: What is the result of 25 − 70 in 8-bit two's complement?
q.why: The answer is −45: 45 = 00101101, inverted 11010010, plus 1 gives 11010011. 10101101 is −45 in sign and magnitude.

q.q: What is 11101100 + 11110001 in 8-bit two's complement, given as denary?
q.why: −20 + (−15) = −35. The sum 1 11011101 has its carry discarded, leaving 11011101 = −128 + 93 = −35.

q.q: While calculating 60 − 23 in two's complement there is a carry out of the most significant bit. What does this mean?
o: The answer has overflowed and must be rejected
It is a normal part of the method and is discarded
The answer is negative and must be inverted
The carry must be added back into the LSB
q.why: In two's complement a carry out of the MSB is simply discarded; overflow is judged from the signs, not the carry.

q.q: 90 and 60 are added in an 8-bit two's complement register. Which value is actually stored?
q.why: 150 is above +127, so the stored pattern 10010110 reads as −128 + 22 = −106: overflow has occurred.

q.q: Which of these additions overflows in 8-bit two's complement?
q.why: −150 is below −128. −64 + (−64) = −128 just fits, and 60 + 67 = 127 just fits.

q.q: Why can adding a positive and a negative number never overflow in two's complement?
o: Any carry out of the most significant bit is simply discarded
The sign bit of the result is always set to 0 by the ALU
The processor clears the overflow flag before such additions
The answer always lies between the two inputs, which are in range
q.why: The result of adding numbers of opposite sign lies between them, so it cannot leave the range.

q.q: A programmer finds that a total kept in an sbyte variable sometimes overflows. What is the best fix?
o: Store the total in hexadecimal instead of binary
Ignore any carry out of the most significant bit
Use sign and magnitude instead of two's complement
Store the total in a wider type such as a 32-bit int
q.why: A wider data type has a larger range (an int reaches over 2 billion), so the true result fits.

q.q: What is 9.375 in unsigned 4.4 fixed-point binary?
What is the two's complement 4.4 fixed-point number 1101.1000 in denary?
q.why: Place values −8, 4, 2, 1, ½ …: −8 + 4 + 1 + 0.5 = −2.5. 13.5 is the unsigned reading.

q.q: What is the largest value in a two's complement 4.4 fixed-point format?
A 16-bit fixed-point format is changed from 8 integer and 8 fraction bits to 10 integer and 6 fraction bits. What is the effect?
o: Greater precision but less range
Greater range but less precision
Greater range and greater precision
No change, as the total is still 16 bits
q.why: Moving the point right gives more whole-number bits (range) but fewer fractional bits (coarser steps).

q.q: Using an 8-bit two's complement mantissa and 4-bit two's complement exponent, what is 0.1101000 0011 in denary?
q.why: Exponent 0011 = 3, so move the point 3 right: 0110.1000 = 4 + 2 + 0.5 = 6.5. 0.8125 is the mantissa alone.

q.q: Using an 8-bit mantissa and 4-bit exponent, both two's complement, what is 1.0110000 0010 in denary?
q.why: The mantissa is −1 + 0.25 + 0.125 = −0.625 and the exponent is 2, so the value is −0.625 × 4 = −2.5.

q.q: Using an 8-bit mantissa and 4-bit exponent, both two's complement, what is 0.1100000 1110 in denary?
q.why: Exponent 1110 = −2, so the point moves 2 left: 0.75 × ¼ = 0.1875. 3 results from treating the exponent as +2.

q.q: What is the value of the two's complement mantissa 0.1010000 on its own?
q.why: The place values after the point are ½, ¼, ⅛ …: 0.5 + 0.125 = 0.625.

q.q: What is 6.75 as a normalised floating-point number with an 8-bit mantissa and 4-bit exponent?
q.why: 6.75 = 110.11 = 0.11011 × 2³, so the mantissa is 0.1101100 and the exponent 0011. 0.0110110 0100 has the same value but is not normalised.

q.q: What is 0.1875 as a normalised floating-point number with an 8-bit mantissa and 4-bit exponent?
q.why: 0.1875 = 0.0011 = 0.11 × 2⁻², and −2 in 4-bit two's complement is 1110.

q.q: What is −5.25 as a normalised floating-point number with an 8-bit mantissa and 4-bit exponent?
q.why: 5.25 = 0.1010100 × 2³; the two's complement of the mantissa is 1.0101100 and the exponent stays 0011. 1.0101011 forgets to add 1.

q.q: When a value is converted to normalised floating point, when does the exponent become negative?
o: When the magnitude of the value is less than ½
Whenever the value being stored is negative
When the magnitude of the value is less than 1
When the mantissa begins with the bits 1.0
q.why: The sign of the value is carried by the mantissa; the exponent is negative only if the point must move right to reach 0.1, i.e. the magnitude is below ½.

q.q: The floating-point number 0.0010110 0110 is normalised. What is the result?
q.why: Shift the mantissa 2 places left to 0.1011000 and subtract 2 from the exponent: 6 − 2 = 4 = 0100.

q.q: The floating-point number 1.1101000 0011 is normalised. What is the result?
q.why: Shift left 2 places until the first two bits differ (1.0…) and subtract 2 from the exponent: 3 − 2 = 1. The value is still −1.5.

q.q: Which of these mantissas is a normalised negative number?
q.why: A normalised negative mantissa starts 1.0, so its first two bits differ.

q.q: Which pair of reasons best explains why floating-point numbers are normalised?
o: Greater range and a smaller total number of bits
Positive values only and faster integer hardware
Exact storage of 0.1 and no rounding errors
Maximum precision and a unique form for each value
q.why: Removing redundant leading bits keeps as many significant bits as possible, and each value then has only one normalised form.

q.q: A 12-bit floating-point format is changed from an 8-bit mantissa and 4-bit exponent to a 6-bit mantissa and 6-bit exponent. What is the effect?
o: Precision increases and range decreases
Both range and precision increase
Neither changes, as the total is still 12 bits
Range increases and precision decreases
q.why: More exponent bits let the point move further (range), but fewer mantissa bits store fewer significant bits (precision).

q.q: What is the largest positive value with an 8-bit two's complement mantissa and a 4-bit two's complement exponent?
q.why: The largest mantissa 0.1111111 times the largest exponent 2⁷ gives 1111111 = 127.

q.q: Which application is best suited to fixed-point rather than floating-point representation?
o: An embedded controller reading a sensor with a known range
A simulation of planets and stars in astronomy
Physics calculations in a 3D computer game
A scientific model of very tiny particles
q.why: Fixed point is fast and simple with constant precision over a small known range; the others need a very wide range.

q.q: In the IEEE 754 standard, how is a 32-bit float divided?
o: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits and 20 mantissa bits
1 sign bit, 23 exponent bits and 8 mantissa bits
1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 mantissa bits
1 sign bit, 7 exponent bits and 24 mantissa bits
q.why: A float has 1, 8 and 23 bits (about 7 significant denary digits); a 64-bit double has 1, 11 and 52.

q.q: 0.1 is stored in unsigned 4.4 fixed point as the nearest available value. What is the absolute error?
q.why: The nearest values are 0.0625 and 0.125; 0.125 is closer, giving |0.1 − 0.125| = 0.025.

q.q: A value that should be 0.2 is stored as 0.1875. What is the relative error?
q.why: Absolute error 0.0125 ÷ true value 0.2 = 0.0625 = 6.25%. 6.67% comes from dividing by the stored value instead.

q.q: Using an 8-bit mantissa and a 4-bit exponent, both two's complement, which value would cause underflow?
q.why: The smallest positive normalised value is about 0.00195, so 0.0001 is too close to zero. Underflow is about tiny magnitudes, not negative numbers.

q.q: Using an 8-bit mantissa and a 4-bit two's complement exponent, which value would cause overflow?
q.why: 200 = 0.11001 × 2⁸, but the largest exponent is +7. 100 = 0.11001 × 2⁷ just fits.

q.q: Which is the best definition of a character set?
o: The set of fonts installed that decide how each character looks
The keys available on a keyboard for a particular language
The binary codes for the digits 0 to 9 used in calculations
The characters a system can represent, each with a unique binary code
q.why: A full definition needs both halves: a list of characters and a unique binary code for each one.

q.q: Which ASCII code is a control character rather than a printable character?
q.why: Codes 0–31 are control characters; 10 is line feed. 32 is space, 48 is '0' and 65 is 'A'.

q.q: A text file sent from one computer shows the wrong symbols on another, even though the bytes arrived unchanged. What is the most likely cause?
o: The parity bits were removed during transmission
The two systems map codes to characters differently
The receiving computer has a lower colour depth
The file was compressed before it was transmitted
q.why: If sender and receiver do not agree on a character set, the same bytes are shown as different characters.

q.q: The ASCII code for 'A' is 65. What is the code for 'g'?
q.why: Lower case starts at 'a' = 97, and 'g' is six letters later: 103. 71 is capital 'G'.

q.q: How many bytes does UTF-8 use to store the name 'Seán'?
q.why: S, e and n are ASCII characters (1 byte each) and an accented letter such as á takes 2 bytes: 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 5.

q.q: Which statement about UTF-8 is correct?
o: It uses between one and four bytes per character
It always uses exactly two bytes per character
It uses seven bits per character, as ASCII does
It always uses exactly four bytes per character
q.why: UTF-8 is variable width: 1 byte for ASCII up to 4 for most emoji. UTF-32 is the fixed four-byte encoding.

q.q: Why does an alphabetical sort that compares ASCII codes place 'Zebra' before 'apple'?
o: The sort compares the last letter of each word first
Lower-case letters are control characters in ASCII
All capital letters have lower codes than lower-case letters
ASCII codes for letters are not in alphabetical order
q.why: Capitals are 65–90 and lower case 97–122, so any capital comes before any lower-case letter.

q.q: A 2000-character document is written in Chinese characters and saved in UTF-8. Approximately how large is the text?
o: 2000 bytes
6000 bytes
4000 bytes
8000 bytes
q.why: Most Chinese characters need three bytes in UTF-8: 2000 × 3 = 6000 bytes.

q.q: Which is an advantage of a fixed-width encoding such as UTF-32 over UTF-8?
o: English text takes up less space than in UTF-8
It can represent more characters than UTF-8 can
The program can jump straight to the nth character
It stays compatible with 7-bit ASCII files
q.why: With every character 4 bytes, position n is at byte 4n; UTF-8 must be scanned from the start. UTF-32 wastes space for English.

q.q: A messaging app must handle English, Greek and emoji in the same message. Which character set is needed?
o: Unicode
ASCII
Extended ASCII
BCD
q.why: Only Unicode covers almost all scripts and emoji; extended ASCII has just 256 codes.

q.q: Using even parity with the parity bit on the left, what byte is sent for the 7-bit data 1001101?
q.why: 1001101 already has four 1s (even), so the parity bit is 0.

q.q: Odd parity is used. Which received byte would be accepted as error-free?
q.why: 10110000 has three 1s (odd). The others have four, four and zero 1s, which are even.

q.q: A byte 01100011 is sent with even parity and arrives as 01010011. What happens?
o: It is rejected, because the count of 1s has become odd
It is accepted, because two flipped bits leave the count of 1s even
It is corrected, because the parity bit locates the error
It is rejected, because the parity bit itself has changed
q.why: Two bits flipped, so the received byte still has four 1s; parity cannot detect an even number of errors.

q.q: One parity bit is added to every 7 data bits, giving bytes. What proportion of the transmission is overhead?
q.why: One bit in every eight carries no data: 1 ÷ 8 = 12.5%. 14.3% is 1 ÷ 7, comparing with data bits only.

q.q: How is the calculation of a check digit different from that of a parity bit?
o: It uses a count of the 1s in each transmitted byte
It uses a weighted calculation on the other digits
It is chosen to make the total of all digits even
It is calculated again only when data is transmitted
q.why: A check digit comes from a weighted calculation such as Modulus 11; a parity bit comes from counting 1s.

q.q: A pupil types a classmate's valid student ID, which includes a correct check digit. Why is the mistake not detected?
o: Check digits only detect errors that occur during transmission
The check digit is checked only when the code is first created
Check digits can only detect transposition errors, not this one
The check digit only shows the code is well formed, not that it is the right one
q.why: A valid code passes the calculation even if it belongs to someone else.

q.q: Why are the digits of a code multiplied by different weights when a check digit is calculated?
o: So that the total is always a multiple of 11
So that the check digit can never be the letter X
So that swapping two digits changes the total
So that the code can be stored as an integer
q.why: With equal weights, a transposition gives the same sum and would go unnoticed; weights make position matter.

q.q: How many colours can be represented with a 24-bit colour depth?
q.why: 2²⁴ = 16 777 216 colours. 16 777 215 is the largest code, not the number of colours.

q.q: A web colour is written #FF8C00. What are its red, green and blue values?
q.why: FF = 255, 8C = 8 × 16 + 12 = 140 and 00 = 0, giving orange.

q.q: A 6 × 4 inch photograph is scanned at 300 dpi. What are its dimensions in pixels?
q.why: Multiply each dimension by the dpi: 6 × 300 = 1800 and 4 × 300 = 1200.

q.q: An image must show 200 different colours. What is the minimum colour depth?
o: 7 bits
200 bits
16 bits
8 bits
q.why: 2⁷ = 128 is too few; 2⁸ = 256 is enough.

q.q: A 4800-byte block of pixel data holds a 1-bit image that is 160 pixels wide. How many pixels high is it?
q.why: 4800 × 8 = 38 400 bits; at 1 bit per pixel that is 38 400 pixels; 38 400 ÷ 160 = 240. 30 forgets to convert bytes to bits.

q.q: Which item of image metadata is EXIF data rather than data needed to rebuild the pixel grid?
o: The width in pixels
The camera model
The colour depth
The height in pixels
q.why: Width, height and colour depth are essential to decode the pixels; EXIF adds date, camera, settings and GPS.

q.q: A school wants to publish pupils' photos on its website. Which metadata should it remove first?
o: The colour depth
GPS location data
The image width
The file format
q.why: Location data could reveal where a pupil lives or is, so it is a privacy risk; the others are needed to display the image.

q.q: What does a vector graphic file store?
o: Objects with properties such as coordinates and fill colour
The colour of every pixel at a fixed resolution
A grid of pixels together with a colour palette
Compressed rows of pixels with an EXIF header
q.why: A vector stores drawing objects and their properties and recalculates them at any size.

q.q: A vector logo is printed at twice its original width and height. What happens to the file size?
o: It doubles
It quadruples
It stays the same
It halves
q.why: A vector's size depends on the number and complexity of its objects, not on the display size.

q.q: A museum is digitising historic handwritten letters with a scanner. Which graphic type should it use?
o: Vector, because it will keep the text sharp when enlarged
Bitmap, because the scanner captures the page as pixels
Vector, because the file size will not depend on resolution
Bitmap, because bitmaps never pixelate when enlarged
q.why: A scan records pixels of continuous detail; it cannot be described efficiently as shapes.

q.q: Human hearing reaches about 20 kHz. According to the Nyquist theorem, what is the minimum sampling rate needed?
o: 20 kHz
40 kHz
10 kHz
44.1 kHz
q.why: The rate must be at least twice the highest frequency: 2 × 20 = 40 kHz. 44.1 kHz is the CD rate, a little above the minimum.

q.q: What is the effect of increasing the sample resolution of a recording?
o: Higher frequencies are captured, but the file is larger
Each amplitude is recorded more precisely, and the file is smaller
Each amplitude is recorded more precisely, but the file is larger
The recording gains a sense of direction, and the file doubles
q.why: More bits per sample give more amplitude levels and less quantisation noise; higher frequencies depend on sampling rate.

q.q: Which is the correct sequence when sound is digitised by an ADC?
o: Measure the frequency, round it, store it as a hex value
Store the voltage, then sample it at random intervals
Sample the binary signal, then convert it to analogue
Sample at regular intervals, measure the amplitude, store it as binary
q.why: The analogue signal is sampled at regular intervals, each sample's amplitude is measured and stored as a binary number.

q.q: What is the size of an uncompressed 1024 × 768 image with 24-bit colour depth?
o: 18 MB

q.q: A 3-minute stereo song is sampled at 44 100 Hz with 16-bit samples. Approximately how big is the uncompressed file?
o: 0.5 MB
q.why: 44 100 × 16 × 2 × 180 = 254 016 000 bits ÷ 8 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 ≈ 30.3 MB. 15.1 leaves out stereo; 0.5 uses 3 instead of 180 seconds.
